extracted.intended_audience: legal practitioners, scholars, policymakers, and informed public interested in First Amendment and tech-platform regulation
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating whether government outreach to social-media platforms (so-called 'jawboning') violates the First Amendment, including doctrinal tests, evidentiary standards, procedural posture, and practical remedies. The page is a Lawfare podcast transcript discussing Murthy v. Missouri and related jawboning and platform-regulation cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coercion versus persuasion (Bantam Books line)
rubrics_metrics.description: The traditional First Amendment line in jawboning cases drawn from Bantam Books: the government cannot coerce intermediaries into suppressing speech, but may persuade them. Lower courts have long treated coercion as unconstitutional and persuasion as permissible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied case-by-case; courts look for conduct that amounts to coercion rather than mere persuasion. Example: Bantam Books involved an informal system of censorship—coercive conduct that was unconstitutional. Courts should evaluate whether government communications are advisory/educational or constitute pressure that overbears private choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plaintiffs' 'no-persuasion' theory
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiffs in Murthy argued that it is unconstitutional for the federal government to try to persuade platforms to take down constitutionally protected speech — i.e., persuasion itself should be prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theory would create a clear bright-line test (advantage: administrability) but would 'undo 60 years of legal precedent' and severely constrain routine, benign, and socially valuable governmental speech and interactions (disadvantage: harms government ability to govern). The podcast notes this as a radical/legal-test alternative and warns of democratic costs if accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-action test (Blum v. Yaretsky) / 'so significantly coerced' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Blum v. Yaretsky, the test for treating private conduct as state action is whether the government 'so significantly coerced or encouraged' the private conduct 'that the choice in law made by the private actor must be deemed to be that of the state.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a stringent test; finding state action subjects private platforms to constitutional constraints. The Fifth Circuit applied a watered-down version (invoking 'encouragement'), which the podcast criticizes as diluting the demanding Blum standard. Courts must be cautious: state-action findings should be rare and require substantial evidence of coercion/entanglement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deference to district-court factual findings on preliminary injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A procedural rule: appellate courts generally owe deference to district-court findings of fact that underlie a preliminary injunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Murthy involved extensive district-court factual findings supporting a broad preliminary injunction; justices questioned how much deference to give, especially where record quality is disputed. Guidance: appellate review should weigh the district court's findings but remain attentive to record flaws, misrepresentations, or motivated reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing and procedural disposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural thresholds such as standing can resolve cases without reaching merits questions about coercion or persuasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government focused on standing during argument; courts may dispose of cases on procedural grounds (e.g., standing) rather than clarifying constitutional doctrine. Parties and courts should assess standing, traceability, and causation early because these can be dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traceability/causation between government contacts and platform removals
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement to trace particular content removals to government pressure or coercion rather than independent platform editorial decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts probe whether alleged removals were 'taken at the behest of the government' or were platform decisions based on their own policies. Lack of traceability undermines plaintiffs' claims; effective pleadings should identify specific instances where government contact led to suppression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality and sufficiency of the evidentiary record
rubrics_metrics.description: The factual record's solidity is central—Murthy arrived at the Court with a 'somewhat shaky evidentiary record' and allegations of factual errors or omissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and advocates should ensure accuracy and completeness of factual submissions. Misstatements can damage credibility (example: justice chastising counsel for misrepresenting facts). A voluminous but error-prone record weakens claims and invites appellate scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit versus implied threats (sensitivity to implied coercion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal evaluation must account for implied threats; prohibiting only explicit threats would permit coercion by implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrine should detect implied threats in context (e.g., 'We're considering our other options' as an implied threat). Tests must be sensitive enough to capture threats that are not overtly phrased, otherwise governments could coerce platforms through indirect wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual, repeat-player, and asymmetry considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessments should consider the broader context: platforms are repeat players, interactions are part of ongoing relationships, and asymmetries (who participates, which level of platform official) matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single communications should be interpreted in light of history, power imbalances, and how the platform is likely to perceive implicit pressure. Courts should evaluate cumulative context rather than isolating specific emails or meetings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric (pattern) versus discrete-instance cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Most jawboning cases challenge discrete, identifiable government contacts; Murthy alleged an 'atmospheric' broad pattern of disparate conduct rather than a handful of plainly coercive acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atmospheric cases are harder to adjudicate because individual interactions may appear benign; plaintiffs must connect the pattern to coercive effect. Courts may struggle to apply coercion/persuasion tests to wide-ranging, diffuse allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy scope and limits (injunction breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies—especially preliminary injunctions—must be narrowly tailored and should not forbid constitutionally permissible interactions between government and platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The district court's preliminary injunction was described as 'extremely broad' (forbidding many interactions), and the Fifth Circuit narrowed it; courts must avoid overbroad relief that chills legitimate governmental or research interactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency as a structural/administrative protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy proposal: require government transparency about interactions with platforms (e.g., publicizing ex parte communications) to deter coercion and enable accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency could make it easier for platforms to publicly push back and for courts and the public to evaluate conduct. Platforms may hesitate to publicize communications for relationship-management reasons; a statutory transparency requirement would shift that burden off platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradeoff: clear bright-line rules versus fuzzy, case-by-case testing
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrinal tradeoff between administrable, bright-line rules (e.g., plaintiffs' no-persuasion test) and the more nuanced, but less predictable, case-by-case coercion inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bright-line rules favor predictability but risk over- or under-protecting speech (and hindering governance). The discussion favors retaining a contextual standard despite its fuzziness, because prophylactic rules could be democratically harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protecting government ability to govern versus protecting speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrinal balancing: rules should permit governments to represent and persuade in political discourse while preventing coercive suppression of protected speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether an outcome would materially impair government's structural need to speak and govern (e.g., advising platforms about public-health risks) against the risk of enabling government control over public discourse. Courts should avoid rules that make ordinary governing communications unconstitutional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of chilling research and public-interest partnerships
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation and unclear doctrine can chill government-platform collaborations and independent research crucial to election security and public-safety monitoring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and policymakers should weigh collateral consequences: overly broad rulings may reduce CISA/FBI/platform cooperation and academic research sharing, leaving society less able to detect and mitigate threats (example: platforms reporting reduced communications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stretching jawboning doctrine to fix platform concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: Jawboning doctrine should not be used as a catch-all to remedy harms caused by concentrated private power; structural competition policy is a different tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The podcast urges caution: concentration of platform power exacerbates jawboning problems, but remedies to concentration (antitrust, structural reforms) are preferable to contorting First Amendment doctrine to address them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credibility and accuracy of briefs and advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocates must ensure factual accuracy in briefs and submissions; misrepresentations can prompt negative judicial reactions and undermine claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Justice Sotomayor accused a plaintiff's lawyer of misrepresenting facts; counsel apologized. Accurate, forthright briefing preserves credibility and reduces risk of adverse rulings based on factual errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platforms' editorial/free-speech rights versus regulation as common carriers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether platforms retain First Amendment editorial rights (and thus protection to set content-moderation policies) or can be regulated as common carriers/neutral conduits is a core inquiry overlapping with jawboning and NetChoice litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding platforms effectively as state actors or removing their editorial protections would have major consequences. Courts should be attentive to the distinct questions of state action and platforms' own First Amendment rights when resolving jawboning claims.
